episodes.171541: High pressure was established across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the evening of August 25th, allowing for only widely-scattered showers and thunderstorm development, mainly confined along and west of the Blue Ridge.  Wind speeds in the lower levels of the atmosphere were generally less than 10 mph from the northwest, supporting only very slow movement of the convection.  Dry air associated with the high pressure limited precipitable water values that evening to 1.23 inches per the August 26th 00Z upper air sounding performed by NWS Blacksburg, which is very near the 50th percentile for late August.  One slow moving thunderstorm developed over northern Roanoke County and tracked slowly southeast along the Botetourt County line.  The storm intensified near the community of Cloverdale and produced heavy rainfall between 8 pm and 10 pm EDT at rates of 2 to locally 4 inches per hour.  Some flooding issues were noted, particularly along Tinker Creek which rose 8 feet in under 2 hours.  While the rainfall was intense and justified the issuance of a flash flood warning given the higher population density of the area, the small footprint of the heavy rain, semi-rural nature of the area impacted and the late evening hour limited evidence of flash flooding in the area.
episodes.171637: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of the 25th over east-central Wyoming, mainly across Converse and Niobrara Counties. These storms produced strong winds, large hail, and large accumulations of hail.
episodes.171932: An isolated severe thunderstorm produced localized wind damage over southern Hardy County.
episodes.172270: An active monsoon season continued to impact Southern California, with multiple days of thunderstorms reported across the mountains from August 22-26. The main hazards were heavy rain and minor debris flows, as well as gusty winds from thunderstorms.
episodes.172591: Surface high pressure was located to the north-northeast over the Carolinas. Aloft, broad troughing over the lower Mississippi Valley and ridging over the Bahamas continued southwesterly flow maintaining the anomalously moist airmass over the area, with PWATs near 2.2 inches. The Atlantic sea breeze slowly shifted inland in the morning and afternoon. A slow-moving storm that developed along the sea breeze boundary sat over eastern Jacksonville dumping 2.70 inches of rainfall within 90 minutes.
episodes.172925: Scattered strong summer storms resulted in a few sightings of waterspouts.
episodes.173104: A persistent upper low over Washington favored ample moisture transport into the area. Shear was fairly limited throughout, hence wind gusts were the main concern with these storms, along with potential for heavy rain. Small hail was expected, but a few reports of severe level hail were relayed.
episodes.173146: An upper level wave moving over the Northern Rockies generated sufficient lift, moisture, and wind shear to initiate a supercell thunderstorm.
episodes.173203: A cluster of marginally severe storms developed along the Missouri River Valley in central South Dakota during the heat of the afternoon. Peak winds associated with these storms was measured at 60 mph in Oacoma.
episodes.173225: A low pressure system spinning over northern Louisiana and southern Arkansas brought several rounds of showers and thunderstorms producing heavy rain to Mississippi August 24th through 25th. This resulted in widespread flooding of roads, homes, and businesses around the state.
episodes.173417: A weak warm front that developed the previous day stalled and began to sag southward towards the Mississippi Coast. At the same time, a very moisture rich atmosphere was already in place as it had been for several days. As storms developed within this conducive environment, daytime heating began to intensify storms moving towards the Mississippi Gulf Coast. Those storms produced very heavy rainfall rates that resulted in flash flooding over portions of Jackson and Harrison counties.
episodes.173473: A typical summertime pattern prevailed with scattered afternoon thunderstorms across the tri-state region. A few storms produced heavy rain with localized flooding.
episodes.173546: A mid level trough just north of the I-85 corridor provided the focus for the development of slow moving thunderstorms. PWAT's near two inches resulted in storms that produced high rainfall rates and flash flooding across northern Montgomery County.
episodes.173696: A very moist (PWATs 2.0+ inches) and unstable (MLCAPE 2000-3000 J/KG) air mass led to a very conducive environment for vigorous thunderstorm activity across portions of southeast California. Thunderstorms first developed across the higher terrain near Joshua Tree National Park as well as across the mountains of Northern Baja California. With the upper-level flow from the west, these thunderstorms moved eastward into Imperial and Riverside counties, moving into the very moist and unstable air mass. Radar estimated rainfall amounts were upwards of 2-3 inches in some areas, with most of the rain falling in less than 2 hours. There were several incidences of flash flooding and wind impacts around the region. The biggest impact of the day was a washout of a section of eastbound lanes along Interstate-10, which is a major throughway for ground traffic between Phoenix, AZ and Los Angeles, CA. This caused major traffic delays and detours.
episodes.173700: A very moist (PWATs 2.0+ inches) and unstable (MLCAPE 2000-3000 J/KG) air mass led to be a very conducive environment for vigorous thunderstorm activity across portions of southwest Arizona. A cluster of thunderstorms developed near Yuma during the mid-afternoon hours leading to flash flooding and damaging winds across the Fortuna Hills area. Thereafter, additional storm complexes developed during the late afternoon and evening hours across portions of Yuma and La Paz Counties, likely due to the combination of terrain lift as well as colliding outflows from the storms that developed earlier in the afternoon across portions of Imperial and Riverside Counties.
episodes.173709: A closed Low over the region shifted over North Idaho and increased instability over the area. The instability mixed with afternoon convection to develop isolated thunderstorms.
episodes.173736: Deep atmospheric moisture and a easterly wind flow led to numerous heavy showers and thunderstorms over SW Florida.
episodes.173806: Monsoon moisture fueled scattered thunderstorms over northwest Arizona. A few storms produced flash flooding and severe weather.
episodes.173807: Monsoon moisture fueled scattered thunderstorms over southeast California. Many storms produced flash flooding, and a few produced severe weather.
episodes.173861: A thunderstorm brought strong wind gusts, blowing down a carport.
episodes.173928: A closed Low over the region shifted over North Idaho and increased instability over the area. The instability mixed with afternoon convection to develop isolated thunderstorms.
episodes.173935: Isolated thunderstorms moved west across southeast Arizona during the afternoon and evening. Localized flash flooding occurred in the Tucson Metro area.
episodes.173949: Isolated thunderstorms moved erratically across southeast Arizona during the afternoon and evening. In the Tucson Metro, localized flash flooding occurred and a landspout was spotted.
episodes.173975: Strong thunderstorms moved over the marine area and produced high winds.
episodes.173978: Heavy rain caused flooding in southwest Alabama.
episodes.173980: A wet pattern continued across the Gulf Coast as additional heavy rain led to numerous flooding reports across southwest Alabama and southeast Mississippi.
episodes.173987: A wet pattern continued across the Gulf Coast as additional heavy rain led to numerous flooding reports across southwest Alabama and southeast Mississippi.
episodes.174006: Enough moisture remained over northern Arizona for a few strong thunderstorms. One of those storms caused flash flooding in the northeast part of the state.
episodes.174062: Weak tornadoes occurred over farm land in the coastal Bend on the 23rd near Driscoll and on the 25th near Edroy. No damage occurred with either tornado.

Interstate-10, a major throughway between Phoenix, AZ and Southern California, had a section of the two eastbound (EB) lanes fully washed out due to flash flooding. Video during the washout appear to show the drainage pipes under the road were overcome and compromised by the magnitude of floodwaters. Radar rainfall estimates in this area were around 2-3 inches, with much of the rain falling in less than 2 hours. The washout occurred a few miles east of State Route 177/Desert Center. Caltrans closed I-10 EB due to the washout. I-10 westbound (WB) was also closed briefly due to an overturned semi-truck and SR-177 had already been closed, due to its own separate flooding impacts and downed power lines, by the time of the I-10 washout. This caused major traffic delays and detours through Eastern Riverside County. One EB detour lane was opened around 0700PST on August 25th after emergency construction and the second EB detour lane was not opened until 2300PST August 27th. Timing of flooding impacts based on radar. No injuries were reported from this event.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVADALEV11) recorded 2.64 inches of rain from a thunderstorm, falling during a 90-minute period between 6:50 pm and 8:20 pm on the 25th. Rainfall rates were at one point observed as high as 4 inches per hour. This is between a 25- and 50-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 estimates.  Runoff from this rainfall entered Tinker Creek.

Rainfall rates were estimated to be as high as 1.7 inches per hour. This is about a 200-year rainfall event per NOAA Atlas 14 estimates. Runoff from this rainfall entered Carvin Creek and eventually Tinker Creek.
